utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to deal with some administrative matters first this morning left over from our last hearing. Mr. Nice, it may be convenient if we begin with at least the discussion on what it is that needs to be resolved this morning. The matters which I have are the final selection of Croatia Rule 92 bis witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McKeon is ready to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Foca transcript witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome is ready to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are there any other matters you want to deal with?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: After that, if I can just mention a couple of things, a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll begin with the 92 bis witnesses. Mr. Kay, you're ready on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I think we can save time because the general point that we've seen run throughout all of the subsequent witnesses has been the issue of the JNA as mentioned within those statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which has been the point that the amici have made on behalf of the accused over the issue of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it may be convenient to deal with it with you going first really, if you're in a position to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: A little bit inconvenient, as I need to find those statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McKeon is probably ready to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I've tried to put these into smaller groups of like witnesses for the convenience of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: First of all, these -- I would note that these are all crime base witnesses, and so to that extent would be cumulative of the testimony of Grujic and Strinovic. The first group, I think, starts with 1086, also includes 1136 and 1191. These I would call, witnesses to ethnic cleansing. Witness 1086 deals with the ethnic cleansing of the Erdut area. Witness number 1136 deals with the ethnic cleansing of Ilok, and Witness 1191 deals with the ethnic cleansing of Bapska. These witnesses are all cumulative of the testimony of [redacted] who dealt with the ethnic cleansing of Lovas. And I would also note that there has been one 92 bis witness already admitted under 92 bis, and that will be Witness C-1126 who dealt with the ethnic cleansing of another witness, so I would group those into one group. The next witness on the list I have would be 1238, which deals with the Lovas minefield incident. We've already heard testimony on that incident from [redacted], and I think the amici at least agrees that this witness is cumulative of his testimony. The next witness I would have would be 1175. This is a witness to the Lovas farms incident, different incident from the Lovas minefield incident. This is the person who buried some of the bodies which were found on that. We have already considered under 92 bis the testimony of C-1154, which was admitted under 92 bis for this incident. And also C-1071, which was admitted under 92 bis. Actually, the testimony under C-1071 and this particular witness deal with the very same victim. It's testimony about the same person. The next group deals with the two incidents at Dalj, paragraphs 50 and 51 of the indictment. That would be Witness C-1185 and Witness C-1215. For this incident, we have testimony in court already from C-025 and C-013, and then admitted under 92 bis already for these incidents are C-1187 and 1140 for paragraph 51 and 1052 for paragraph 50. Finally, the last group I have would be three witnesses, 1162, 1055, and 1089. These witnesses all deal with Arkan and killings that the indictment alleges were committed by Arkan's men. Witness 1162 will identify other -- was arrested by Arkan and will identify other prisoners who were held by Arkan including some of the victims named in our indictment. C-1055 will testimony that after one of the victims was arrested, the very next day he was told to move into the victim's house, indicating some knowledge that the victim was not going to come back. And then, finally, C-1089 deals with Klisa. He was arrested but later released and will be able to identify some of the victims. And I think that's the entire list, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. McKeon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've now moved on since the original filing by the amici curiae, and a number of these place are now familiar, so we cannot dispute that they represent a cumulative basis of the evidence of the Prosecutor. The issue that remains is that of cross-examination which we contend should be permitted to the accused to cross-examine upon the issues that are important to his case, and within the issues that are relevant to the indictment is the issue of the JNA, and we have already made objections in relation to that matter which the Trial Chamber has ruled upon and permitted cross-examination, and so that applies again to this batch of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Does it apply to all of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It applies to -- I don't actually have my sheet here with me, Your Honour, I apologise for that, but off my memory, it applies to all, save two, witnesses who didn't mention the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I note 1089, 1162.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. It was -- two witnesses was my memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 1185. I don't know if you have your note to look at over the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I can try and locate it. We moved courts as you recollect on the last Thursday which put me in a bit of difficulty but it was two witnesses alone from my memory that did not mention the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I have to say about those witnesses again from my memory, they were very general cumulative witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, on that particular issue, is there anything you want to add to what's already been said?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know, Mr. May, yourself, my basic objections, and I assume that you have managed to read through the statements, although I don't know the time you have at your disposal to do that. But I assume that you found yourself that all the things that those witnesses say has nothing to do with the authorities of Serbia or myself. So I don't really understand why we have to listen to the witnesses about all the terrors of the war and all the terrible things that happened during the war but had nothing to do with Serbia. But that's up to you. That's the way you work. It's become standard practice here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll move next to deal with the different issue which is the Foca witnesses who gave evidence in other proceedings, a total of 11, who were first of all cross-examined; secondly, of course, gave evidence on oath in those proceedings. So it may be that different principles apply. The Trial Chamber again will have under the Rule to decide, first of all, whether to admit the transcripts, and if they are admitted whether the witnesses should be called for cross-examination, although they had been cross-examined in the earlier proceedings. The issue, no doubt, will be as to whether there are other issues, any other issues, on which they should be cross-examined. We've read the written submissions on this subject, so there's no need to repeat those. Yes, Mr. Groome. Perhaps you could introduce the matter generally. It may be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The 11 witnesses whom the Prosecution has referred to and similarly the Chamber as the Foca witnesses are 11 witnesses who testified in the cases of Prosecutor versus Kunarac and Prosecutor versus Krnojelac. In this case you have ruled on 92 bis already with respect to a similar submission regarding eight witnesses from the Dokmanovic case. I will tailor my remarks regarding these witnesses to address the criteria articulated as the basis of your consideration and decision with respect to those Dokmanovic witnesses. Namely, the proximity of the witness's testimony to the acts and conduct of the accused and therefore its admissibility under 92 bis (D). And secondly, whether or not these witnesses should be called for additional cross-examination by this accused. If I may begin with, Your Honour, the two witnesses B-1542 and B-1543. They both testified in the Kunarac case and were known in that case as FWS-75 and FWS-87 respectively. B-1542, in addition to providing general evidence about the takeover of Foca, describes her experience of being repeatedly raped and abused over a period of three months, and she described her personal knowledge of similar acts against other women and girls. B-1543 tells of a similar account of her captivity and repeated rape by several men over the course of two months. With respect to the first inquiry regarding proximity, there can be no reasonable view that the evidence of these two women is proximate in any way to the direct acts of the accused. It was not the theory of the Prosecution case that this accused was in any way directly responsible in the actual commission of those crimes or had any direct authority over those who physically perpetrated the crimes. It is our theory that although very remote from these crimes, his participation in a joint criminal enterprise as defined in the indictment facilitated and resulted in foreseeable crimes like these to occur. With respect to a consideration of whether these witness should be required to appear before this Chamber for additional cross-examination by the accused. Before I address this question with particular respect to these two witnesses, I would like to make some general submissions regarding this question. The Prosecution fully recognises that the attendance and cross-examination of witnesses is one of the most important rights afforded an accused and also ensures the legitimacy and accuracy of any decision ultimately reached by a Trial Chamber, that right clearly being enshrined in Article 21. But directly following Article 21 is Article 22, the importance of a Trial Chamber to consider the impacts of proceedings on victims and witnesses that appear before it. What was not specifically dealt with in your consideration of the Dokmanovic witnesses, which I submit should be part of your consideration of these Foca witnesses, is the impact of requiring these witnesses to attend for additional cross-examination. It is the Prosecution's submission that should the Chamber balance the need to protect these witnesses against whether that protection unfairly impinges upon the rights of the accused will be clear that in the case of these two witnesses, they should not be required to appear for cross-examination. B-1542, after providing her testimony on examination-in-chief was fully cross-examined by three different Defence counsel regarding her testimony. Over 150 pages of transcript were consumed in this exercise. Similarly, B-1543 was cross-examined by four different Defence counsels for a total of over 100 pages of transcript. The Chamber has recently heard the testimony of B-1405 who suffered similar crimes and fresh in our memory must be the difficulty and the pain which such testimony exacts upon the victims who must give it. It is our position that nonetheless, if renewed cross-examination can reasonably be believed to assist the Chamber in its determination of a significant issue in this case, the Prosecution agrees such witness should be required to attend. Conversely, if no such reasonable belief exists, it is the Prosecutor's position that the mandate of Article 22 requires that witnesses not be brought to attend additional cross-examination. In the case of these two witnesses and other witnesses, there is no reasonable expectation that additional cross-examination will be of any assistance to the Chamber. If I might add parenthetically, as indicated also in our written submission, B-1543 does not believe that she could endure additional cross-examination, and it is not the Prosecutor's intention at this time to request a subpoena or in any way attempt to compel her to appear. We would withdraw her as a witness. What the accused's position will be with respect to these two women, I expect it will likely be as in the past that he will broadly oppose these procedures that have been designed to facilitate efficient proceedings while protecting his rights and interest. In the event that he does not indicate how the previous cross-examination was inadequate or what additional areas he would seek to question the witness regarding, the Prosecution submits the following: We have now been in trial for over one year. Clear patterns of cross-examination have emerged. Absent his willingness to state with particularity what areas of questions he seeks to put to these two witnesses, I submit the Chamber's analysis should include those areas of examination he regularly and consistently engages in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us consider the submission. You say that although there is no specific reference in the Rule, nonetheless a Chamber, in deciding whether a witness should be called for further cross-examination, should take into account the likely effect upon a witness who has suffered traumatic events as these witnesses have. Anyone who has read that transcript will see. On the other hand, you can see that it will be right for a Chamber to consider cross-examination if there was some issue, some significant issue which wasn't addressed in the earlier cross-examinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We do not place them on a par, the rights of the victims on a par with the right of the accused to face his accuser, but simply a matter to be considered. If there is no reasonable expectation that further cross-examination will shed new light on a new issue or on an issue not adequately covered that the Chamber would be entitled to not require the witness to attend for additional cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's the modern trend to take account of the impact on witnesses of being made to appear in court and retell their events, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Especially in cases of sexual assault and of such extended and prolonged sexual assault as in these two cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was beginning to say I was going to use as an example the Chamber I think is entitled to look back at the year history of this trial and to evaluate the types of cross-examination that the accused has engaged in when evaluating whether witnesses being brought here and subjected to similar cross-examination, whether that will be of assistance to the Chamber, and I would use as one example the accused routinely explores inconsistencies between witnesses in-court testimony and prior statements. The Chamber -- if the Chamber examines in the case of both B-1542 and B-1543, that this was done with facility and adequately in the previous trial by a number of different Defence attorneys. There is no reasonable belief at present that the accused will be in a position to more fully exploit the differences that exists between the prior statement and the in-court testimony of those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it may be said that that point can be made in relation to all the -- virtually all the witnesses, that their previous statements were put to them. Not just these two but other witnesses too, I think I'm right in saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That will be our position, Your Honour, when I with the other witnesses. It would be the same position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And one can get some idea of the extent of the cross-examination, maybe not the detail, of course, because it's a very rough-and-ready test by the pages which were taken up with cross-examination. I notice in the case of the last witness you mentioned, 1543, was cross-examined, I take it, for 102 pages as against 67 for direct or examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If it is of assistance to the Chamber, we would be willing to point with particularity the specific references in the cross-examination that dealt with such things such as impeachment with prior statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm prepared to do that today. We would prepare a chart overnight and submit it to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Another avenue that the accused routinely explores with witnesses is parts of their testimony which appear illogical or improbable. A cursory examination of both of these cross-examinations will indicate that this also was done at length and with some facility by the different Defence attorneys that questioned these witnesses. Finally, the accused routinely puts to witnesses information and facts that he has in his possession that he believes furthers his position in the hope that the witness may be in a position to confirm those facts. It was the Prosecution's submission, as the Chamber regularly reminds the accused, that this is a matter more properly dealt with on the Defence case in due course, and it would be the Prosecution's position that a witness should not be brought back for additional cross-examination in the hope that that witness might be able to confirm a fact which the accused wishes to put before the Chamber. One final matter with respect that these witnesses, Your Honour is that the Prosecution is not in possession of any additional Rule 68 material tending to impeach these witnesses that was not available to the original cross-examiners. The Prosecution submits that if the Chamber engages in this analysis, it is clear that in the case of B-1542 and B-1543, that they should not be required to attend cross-examination absent the accused or the amici putting forth some articulable basis that additional cross-examination could be reasonably believed to yield some new evidence or be of some assistance in the Chamber's determination of a significant issue in this trial. In the absence of that, it is the Prosecution's contention that the testimony should be admitted without cross-examination. As a measure of additional caution, with respect to protecting the rights of the accused, the Prosecution would not oppose a later application by the amici or the accused later in the trial asking the Court to reconsider this matter if it should appear towards a later point in the trial that some important issue was raised by these witnesses and it would appear at that stage that additional cross-examination could shed light on that additional issue. The Prosecution would not oppose the Chamber reopening its consideration of this matter. I apologise with taking so long with these two witnesses. I will deal with the remaining nine in a far more expeditious manner. The next witnesses I would like to deal with are B-1015, B-1533, B-1618, and B-1120. Some of those witnesses were protected in the Foca trial, so I would refer to all of them by their assigned witness pseudonyms. In that case, they were respectively FSW-104, FSW-15, FSW-33, FSW-111. The subject of the testimony of all these witnesses concerns the circumstances surrounding the takeover of Foca as well as the conditions in the KP Dom. It is the Prosecution's position that none of their testimony is sufficiently proximate to the acts and conduct of the accused as to make it inadmissible under 92 bis (D). With respect to the question of cross-examination, I submit the following: The Prosecution filed this motion before any of the Chamber's recent 92 bis decisions. What has emerged from the Chamber's rulings, as the law of this case, is that witnesses that offer evidence regarding the JNA touch upon an important issue raised by the accused and, therefore, should appear for cross-examination. The Prosecution concedes that if the Chamber is inclined to follow this analysis, then these witnesses do speak to the participation of the JNA or the use of its facilities and would be appropriately called for limited purpose of cross-examination on that issue. With respect to cross-examination on other issues, it is the Prosecution's submission that such should not be allowed. All four witnesses were subjected to extensive cross-examination on inconsistencies between their in-court testimony and their prior statements. All were cross-examined regarding those portions of their testimony the Defence deemed improbable. B-1618 was cross-examined by each of the counsel of the three accused. With respect to B-1536, the Prosecution's position is similar. The witness does talk about paramilitaries from Serbia taking part in the attack on Foca including Seselj's men and Arkan's Tigers. Again the Prosecution concedes that if the Chamber is to apply its same analysis that it did with respect to its March decision on the JNA, then the presentation of paramilitary forces from Serbia may raise sufficiently similar issues that similarly limited cross-examination would seem appropriate. It is the Prosecution's position that such renewed cross-examination should be strictly limited to this issue. Again, this witness was cross-examined by four different Defence counsel in two trials. The final group of witnesses I would ask to deal with are B-1121, B-1537, B-1538, and B-1540. Respectively they were known in the Foca trials as FSW-111, FSW-109 -- sorry, FWS-69, and FWS-54. This last group of witnesses address in general terms the outbreak of the conflict in Foca and describe with particularity the conditions of the KP Dom detention facility. There is no reasonable view of their evidence that such evidence is proximate to the conduct of the accused. And is clearly within the ambit of the 92 bis (D). With respect to the issue of cross-examination, all of these witnesses were subjected to thorough and extensive cross-examination. Attempts were made to impeach some of them through questions regarding their participation in the SDA political party. One witness was questioned about a previous psychiatric illness that affected that witness's memory, and other important matters for a trier of fact to be aware of in evaluating their testimony. It is the Prosecution's submission that none of these witnesses directly implicate an important issue raised by the accused in this trial and as such should not be required to attend for additional cross-examination by the accused. I would note parenthetically that in the case of B-1537, the Prosecution has been unable to locate this witness in recent months, and the Prosecution would at this stage seek leave to amend our application for admission of his testimony to be considered under 92 bis (C) instead of (D). Of course, we will continue to look for him and advise the Chamber and the parties of any change in circumstance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you're going to put an application under 92 bis (C) you'll have to put some evidence, or at least a statement or something of that sort in front of us so we have something to consider.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you want to do that, of course do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. I will prepare a submission regarding the efforts made to contact this witness. In conclusion, Your Honour, it is the Prosecution's position that the considerations of Rule 22 are entirely appropriate for consideration when the Chamber considers Rule 92 bis issue of cross-examination. Attendance and questioning in this court impacts all witnesses over a spectrum of mere convenience to hardship to actual trauma in some cases. We submit that the Chamber duly considers this factor, there will be and are in this case those occasions in which there is no reasonable expectation that additional cross-examination will yield new significant information and that no significant impingement of the rights of the accused can said to have been occurred by not requiring such witnesses to attend for a second cross-examination by the accused. To summarise our position in the case of B-1542, B-1543, B-1121, B-1537, 1538, and 1540, it is our request that their testimony be admitted into this trial without the opportunity for the accused to ask them further questions and that doing so is not a violation of his right to cross-examine or the general right to a fair trial. We further acknowledge that if the Chamber is to employ a similar analysis to its ruling of the 27th of March, 2003, that that would require B-1015, 1120, 1533, 1618, and 1536 to attend for limited cross-examination. The Prosecution, however, submits that such cross-examination should be strictly limited to the issue raised by the accused, namely the presence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You referred earlier to Rule 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's confusing. No doubt you meant Article 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My apologies. Your Honour. Article 22 of the Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Concerned with the rights of the victims, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. The due consideration of the rights and the cost to the victims of participating in trials before this Tribunal. So with respect to those witnesses, although the Prosecution acknowledges that it may be appropriate to call them for a limited issue, it is the Prosecution's position that the cross-examination should be strictly limited and would request that any decision with respect to those witnesses by this Chamber include the limitations of the cross-examination to those issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you offered to produce a table overnight of cross-examination matters such as inconsistencies. We think that will be helpful if would you do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the two that I propose would be the use of prior inconsistent statements and questions about the improbability of the testimony. Are there any other areas that the Chamber would be of assistance to identify and locate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I think those are the main areas. Thank you. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The accused has asserted on many occasions during the course of his trial his desire to question witnesses at every opportunity. This is a matter that we are dealing with now that lies within the discretion of the Trial Chamber, and I ask the Court to bear in mind the way that the accused has presented his case and the statements that he has made as to his need to have publicly heard the evidence against him, and we submit that that is an important consideration within any trial when you are dealing with the concept of fairness to an accused. As has already been said, the accused has a right to a fair and public trial under Article 21, subarticle 2 of the Statute of this Tribunal. In the context of his trial, these 11 witnesses would not have been heard in public. Under that same Article 21, the accused has a right to be tried in his presence and defend himself in person. Cross-examination and the questioning in direct examination of those witnesses would not have been in his presence. He would not have been able to observe the demeanour, other personal characteristics of those witnesses, and for him, the relevance of that testimony cannot be assessed, for him, adequately as having been within previous proceedings for other defendants, facing other charges and in a completely different context to his trial. Under that same Article 21, the accused has a right to examine or have examined those witnesses on his behalf that come forward to give testimony against him. Those are the principles that we derive from the Statute that seek to provide a fair trial for an accused. Having stated those principles, it is important now to stress the reasons. The reasons why we have this public hearing, that we give an opportunity to the accused to present his case and to question witnesses and to hear personally himself what is said in the context of his trial against him, the reason why that which has been said in other trials would be inadequate for him is because previous questions would not have been in the context of his case. Previous questioners in cross-examination would not have been questioning on instructions from him, and the importance of cross-examination by other questioners always depends upon the context of that particular individual who at that time is in court and on trial. It may serve the interests in other cases of those cross-examining not to pursue interests or lines of questioning that would be of relevance to this accused, i.e., it is a self-serving process entirely. And those questioning in the previous proceedings would have been serving the interests solely of those accused on trial and not the interests of Mr. Milosevic. They are not mutual interests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You seem to be saying that there are no circumstances under which this particular Rule could ever be applied. And therefore, really what you're saying is that we should ignore it because these general observations could apply to any trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: They are rules of -- a rule of discretion that we submit should be used sparingly. They should not be used wholesale because they may diminish the public nature of a trial. They may diminish in that way to highlight the interests of a particular accused, and by that I mean this accused. And it is worthy of note that the Rule itself was not a founding rule of this Tribunal. It is something that came in later. At the time of the creation of this Tribunal it was not envisaged, I would submit, that this would be the way that proceedings would be conducted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It wasn't envisaged no doubt that the trials would take as long and there would be as much evidence, but that may be a totally different point. I mean, the fact that the founders didn't foresee these problems I don't think is a strong point, I may say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why I mentioned it is that the founders were probably working very closely with the principles in mind from the Statute. And it's easy to envisage situations where the principles of the statute that gives birth to the Tribunal in the first place may become obscured for reasons of expediency and thereby deprive an accused of that important right which underwrites the whole process of the fair trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You see, that depends on a view that all the trial should be oral, and no doubt that was partly in the minds of the founders who gave a primacy to oral evidence, and that's what's been changed. All evidence now is treated equally. Now, I accept, of course, that this is a particular point dealing with evidence in other cases, but one has to take into account the size of the cases and the amount of evidence which is nowadays put before the Tribunal, and what is required is to find an expeditious but fair way of admitting it, and that's why evidence in written form is now more freely admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In a way, judging by the number of pages as to whether a job has been done or not, I would submit to the Tribunal, can be a very inaccurate way of assessing whether evidence has been properly challenged. Page numbers are no guide. It's quality rather than quantity which may be a far more important way of determining how well a job has been done. We do make this point, that Witness B-1015, at the start of cross-examination by Defence counsel refused to cooperate, not answer questions, and was antagonistic. This led, perhaps, but it's a fact on the record, to the Defence counsel putting obviously inaccurate facts in cross-examination and being criticised by a Trial Judge for it. And this highlights the problem in using testimony from other trials where the interests of the parties are not mutual, that the people performing their functions within the trial process are different, that case strategies may be entirely different. Each trial strategy for each accused has to be considered as an entirely self-serving process. And I don't mean that in a derogatory fashion, but it is a fact in the way that they have to contest the proceedings. I take the observation by the Trial Chamber that the points I am raising are critical of this particular Rule, but we stress here that this is a rule that should be used sparingly and not in a wholesale application. At the end --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It seems to me, Mr. Kay, that what you are saying is that this is a rule which if not applied very, very carefully can be ultra vires of the statute in terms of the right to a public hearing and the right of the accused to examine evidence that has been given against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exactly, so, Your Honour. Our submission is that this has forced the principles in a direction too far as far as those principles were the embodiment and the embedding of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, let's be specific. Could you make further observation as to those two witnesses, rape victims, 1542 and 1543? What will be your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: My position is very clear. In relation to any crimes, they should be treated with due equality. And if you start constructing a process that permits certain types of crime to be more easily proved against an accused than another type of crime, again you are moving away from the founding principles of the Tribunal, which -- which addresses victims generally and in full equality without distinguishing between one class and another. As yet, there has been no medical evidence of any harm that the Judges should consider to determine an appropriateness in revising the usual procedures for the giving of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you saying that this is not a matter we should take into account? And secondly, are you really saying that we need medical evidence to consider the possible traumatic effect of a rape victim having to come back and give evidence of a series of rapes? Surely no court needs evidence of that sort. And the final point is this: It's not a question of a separate category here. It's merely a question of whether a witness having given what must have been traumatic evidence, or must have been traumatic for them, should be forced to come back to be further cross-examined. And whatever you say about the equality of cross-examination, certainly the quantity is relevant when considering the length of time they must have already spent in the witness stand. Are you saying we should not take these matters into account when we consider whether we should order cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am sympathetic to any victim who suffered any crime, and that includes those victims of sexual crimes. And it is easy to comprehend the trauma that such victims may later experience in a courtroom. But the issue we have here is that an accused is on trial whose liberty is at stake, and for him the manner and delivery of evidence may be important. It has to be noted certainly in those parts of the trial to date where we have heard such evidence that the accused has been sympathetic and has stated no desire or wish to compound unpleasantness on the witness. So I don't want this issue to be seen as whether it's the amicus curiae, Mr. Kay in particular, forcing this issue onto those victims of rape. It's not the point that I am trying to deal with. I am still wrestling with the underlying problem of testimony that has been given elsewhere in different circumstances against a different accused who has different interests, a different lawyer and a different context for his trial. So there is no desire from this part to use this as an exercise of unpleasantness or harm to a victim, and we consider those Articles within the Statute as being very important which consider the rights of the victims. But the issue here does remain the public nature of the trial which this accused has put forward as being a very important issue in relation to not only his trial but those watching it who may be potential witnesses of whom he has frequently made the point he has no fear or no need to disguise the case against him in any way. One can consider it in a different way against a different accused who is not so prominent, does not feature so highly in the scheme of things, and issues such as this, if he wasn't mentioned in relation to the evidence, carry no importance. Having appeared in another trial myself, I can readily say that, that you let things go by because it makes no difference to your indictment -- your client at that time, and the issues you are following are for a particular accused, to meet the particular case against him. But in relation to this accused and his pronouncements and strategy, one can readily see that his perception of the trial and what he requires to do is very different for his own interests. If I could just turn now to the exhibits, the witness statements. It seems in that trial, for no good reason that I could see of reading the transcripts, that the witness statements went in as a matter of course in direct examination upon the witness being produced by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which trial was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The Foca trial. I have terrible difficulty -- Kunarac and Krnojelac. I apologise to him for my poor pronunciation. I haven't got to that part of the course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're saying both of them. In both of them the statements went in. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. It was a matter of routine. And in that way exhibited material goes onto the record, burnt onto the record, should I say, if it's to be reused, with many aspects within those statements which are not challenged or dealt with in direct or cross-examination. That's a very different state of affairs from the position where a witness produces a map, a photograph, a plan as part of his testimony and one could see why exhibited such material makes sense to the transcript as a whole. But if witness statements go in like that, we can see a back-door route for the admission of statement evidence without any proper hearing upon the contents. And as we know, there are many inaccuracies. How they come about is not for me to say. It's just the fact that there are inaccuracies that need to be mentioned because they affect the reliability. And if the reliability of evidence is affected, the quality of the trial diminishes. So the second strand of our submission is that there be cross-examination by the accused in any event. If the Trial Chamber does not accede to our argument on the matter but permits the transcript testimony in on behalf of the Prosecutor, our fall-back position on his behalf or what we would say is an argument open, a second strand, is that there be cross-examination. I don't know if I can assist any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Mr. Kay. Although, just one final point. I suppose we will have to look, if we were minded to admit any of the transcripts, we would have to look at the witness statements to see whether they were admitted in or not. It would be open to us to exclude the witness statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. It becomes a tricky exercise in my submission, going down that route. It's just when the witness stands up, his statement, "any objections," the Presiding Judge says, the Defence say no and it just goes in like that almost like a tool of the process rather than an evidence in the process, if I can make that distinction if that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic, on this particular point of these transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, precisely on that particular point and separate issue, Mr. May. Just like in all the other aspects, things here are being put topsy-turvy, upside down. The question is not whether the cross-examination has been conducted or not, it's a reversal of thesis. The question is how it was conducted and done and what one wishes to prove in each individual case. Mention is made here of a proposal according to which the facts should be accepted, facts which have been adjudicated in front of this illegal court of yours, and neither you, although you are an illegal Tribunal, did not adjudicate facts but persons, people. You judged upon people. So it was not facts that were adjudicated and that the proposal is they be brought to your knowledge formally, but what we're dealing with are facts that refer to whether or not something took place, where, under what conditions and circumstances and whether a person perpetrated a crime or act of any kind. That was the subject of your deliberations. In the cases which you now wish to put into one box, into one trial, which in itself is cumulative, if I can put it that way, and which represents a completely novel practice in general in trials of any kind, or adjudication or judgement of any kind, which is not surprising as this is an illegal Tribunal. So from your aspects, precisely from your own aspects, as you consider yourself to be a court, you have adjudicated, judged persons and not facts. And you have judged them on the basis of facts which in those proceedings, the legal proceedings conducted against those persons were considered to be adjudicated, which means that adjudicated facts can only be those which refer to whether a certain person did commit a crime of some kind, where, when, against whom, under what circumstances and conditions. Any other facts cannot be considered to have been adjudicated. Mr. Kay, you mentioned a moment ago economics of time, expediency, and that principle does indeed exist. I do not challenge that. I do not challenge its existence. But I assume that you're not going to allow yourself to challenge the fact that when we're talking about legal courts and legal trials, this must not be at the detriment of justice. You usually tend to look at the clock and you're interested in the time, the passage of time mostly. A legal court of law must be interested in justice, that -- justice being done as opposed to principle of expediency and economy in itself. So take a look now at what you have here before you, and putting it mildly, they are dubious facts, and dubious facts can be considered to be adjudicated, which curtails the right for me myself to be able to state my views on those facts or by applying them, by applying the means and resources that I have at my disposal, although you're trying to tie my hands at such as possible in that respect, I wish to put into question and to prove and show before the public that they have not been properly ascertained and adjudicated that, they are the result of insufficient knowledge in certain subject matters and areas, that they have been construed, for example, and even, I would as far as to say, that their assertion emerged from a compromise of the accused and their Defences with the opposite side over there, bargaining with that side over there that calls itself the Prosecution. And that is why that opposite side and this practice seems to be a sort of malignant body and acts in that way in a legal system which is being created and legal thought that is being created, because the eyes of the public see how many compromises are being struck here and bargains that are being struck with different people who are accused here, who are told to own up to certain crimes for them to receive shorter prison terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are well away from the point on which you must address us. The issue is not that of the adjudicated facts, and your hands are not tied, as you know, as far as the evidence is concerned. Providing it's relevant, you can call relevant evidence. But the matter that we are having to consider now and on which we have invited you to address us is the issue of the transcripts which were admitted in the two cases which have been mentioned, and the issue that we're having to determine, there are 11 of them, is whether we should admit them in these -- in this particular case with or without cross-examination. Now, that's the issue which you've got to address.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's the issue I'm talking about, and I believe that I'm taking up less time than the opposite side and the amicus. I don't suppose you're going to challenge, Mr. May, are you, and gentlemen generally, one and all, that there is a complete difference of interests of persons who were judged here and the transcript of which you wish to introduce because it was not in their interests to deal in any depth with certain issues. And as we are talking here about a general -- the general culprit as Serbia is a general culprit and all the territories of Yugoslavia, this seems to be quite a different principle and approach here in order to establish the truth wherein culpability is concerned. What I'm doing, I'm doing for one goal, to establish the truth and the place and of role of my own people in the historical events which came to pass and which you are trying to represent in the way you are here to determine culpability. So it is quite logical to me that in the individual cases people had no interest in delving into any kind of historical and various other circumstances. And I wish to repeat once again. I have already said that the indictment is false and that I will break down all its allegations, and I will be able to do that if you do not curtail my right and time to be able to put that into effect. Now, whether something is essential or not essential, you must allow me to assess that. And everything is essential. Everything is of substance, because everything that took place on the territory of the former Yugoslavia you link to Serbia, its institutions, and to myself personally. So you cannot say that you can exclude something because it is not relevant. Everything is relevant because everything is linked together. And you link it together, even the rapes. Any drunken fool can carry out rapes in London or your own Jamaica, Mr. Robinson, or anywhere else. And I'm sure you're not going to bring the head of state to court because a criminal perpetrated a crime or raped somebody. However, everything is in play here, everything comes into play, and you have presented all kinds of accusations here for things that neither Serbia nor I have anything to do with and for which it is the people who committed the crime against Yugoslavia are to be held accountable and responsible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let me understand it. In relation to the rapes, you might not so much want to question the fact of the rape as you might wish to question who committed it. Do I understand you correctly? You might not wish to question the fact of the rape, that there was a rape, that these women were raped, but you might want to address the issue as to who committed the rapes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I might even question the facts. If my information tells me that a witness statement and testimony is false, Mr. Robinson. Because here there have been a large number of false witnesses. You saw here somebody who said he was a close associate of mine. That's what he claimed, and I've never set eyes on him in his life before. So, Mr. Robinson, you ever introduced into evidence as an exhibit a photograph of a shirt with three holes in it, which Miljazin Tachi, a witness brought in here who said he was shot with a heavy machine-gun from a distance of three metres and that he wasn't wounded because God saved him, God just didn't save his shirt. So you accept quite unbelievable things here in this court. I have received here quite a lengthy document here which says it is a proposal on the part of the Prosecution for note to be taken of adjudicated facts. This is quite nonsensical, because facts were not adjudicated or judged. It was individuals that were judged in a completely different context. And secondly, when it comes to these facts, there are such idiocies here in the historical sense, the factual sense, and any other sense which quite simply you won't need any effort to challenge, one wouldn't need any effort to challenge. They deal with everything, all things together. Several centuries ago the Serbs inhabited the northern and southern areas of Bosnia. That's what the other side claims there. They delve in history. They reshape and recut history. And it delves into all other different things. It says: "Immediately after the First World War and the disintegration of the Habsburg Empire," this is what it says, "a kingdom was created of the Serbs, Croats and Slovenes through the unification of the Kingdom of Serbia with Montenegro, with Croatia, Slovenia and Bosnia-Herzegovina." That's what it says here. Well, neither Croatia nor Bosnia-Herzegovina existed because they're part of the Habsburg Empire. So what kind of unity or unification are we talking about here? These are historical, nonsensical things. They've written nonsense here, a whole book of it. A whole book of facts we have here. And there's another thing they say here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, as the Presiding Judge indicated, we are already through with the issue of adjudicated facts. Please confine yourself to the issue of the transcripts. And in answer to my colleague Judge Robinson's question, you said that you may challenge the fact that -- whether there was a rape or not. May I take it that you are challenging these two witnesses, 1542 and 1543, were raped or not? Could you make your specific observations as to those two witnesses?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, I really do rate very highly your well-intentioned efforts, but I can give an answer to that question only when I have all the facts which are related to their testimony which has not been available to me so far, because within the framework of my time constraints I have to deal with current witnesses, the order of which as you yourself know undergoes change on an almost daily basis, so that this type of practice also makes it more difficult for me or anybody to become better acquainted with this. I do not wish to insult anyone here, Mr. Kwon, but I myself do not believe that anyone, you or Mr. May or Mr. Robinson have managed to read through the 400.000 pages which have been disclosed so far because I just do not see the time that you have to do so in addition to your sitting here and all your other obligations that you have to attend to and, of course, the breaks that you are entitled to. So I don't think that any human being would be able to read through that number of pages but that is why you do consider that you're able to assess what it says there without being fully informed about what it says in all those pages. Take a look at what they say here: With the constitution of 1974, the Muslim population of Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we cannot allow time to go like this. The matter we are discussing here and we are inviting your submissions is about these Foca transcripts. We're not going over the history all over again. Now, is there anything you want to say? We will consider, of course, whether to admit these transcripts and whether to allow cross-examination. Is there anything more you want to say on that issue, on that issue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am absolutely opposed to the fact that any kind of transcripts are introduced into evidence here because it is completely incompatible with the contents of what that false indictment is accusing me of having committed. And they would now like to link it all up into different parcels and packages, different judgements brought under conditions which were suspect, under pressure exerted on people, under conditions of compromise with the accused, bargain pleas and all the rest of it. And they want to put it into one parcel, to tie it up and then to have that represent a crime base or a basis of documents which are all suspect. So I categorically reject any possibility of that being done and I hope that I have expounded that sufficiently clearly and you can decide whichever way you like, because I wouldn't be surprised of any of your decisions. They would not surprise me either way, whichever way it goes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May I make just one correction. It was in relation to the exhibited witness statements. I must have been suffering from transcript fatigue. I was thinking of the Dokmanovic trial where they went in as a matter of course, and I've been able to check it and it was the wrong Tribunal, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I may just briefly, Your Honour. I think there were some witness statements accepted in this case. The Prosecution would not oppose just a simple rejection. It has been the practice -- simple rejection of that has not been the practice of this Trial Chamber. We certainly would not oppose that. I think that raises --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When you do your table about cross-examination, perhaps you could indicate your view about the witness statements in each case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If there had been any which have gone in, well then I think they should be excluded unless they're in for a particular reason which they may be to deal with inconsistencies and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. A similar issue has been raised here with respect to B-1015 and just the general nature of 92 bis. The Prosecution is equally bound by the transcript. There is no requirement in 92 bis that the Chamber accept the evidence. It's simply that the evidence be presented. It's simply about presentation of evidence, that the evidence be presented by transcript as opposed to live testimony. The Chamber would be certainly entitled after reviewing the transcript of the 1015 to combined the witness incredible. The Chamber would be entitled to review any of the exhibits tendered and say they are unreliable. Similarly with the rape. The witness would be able to read the testimony of that rape victim and decide that the Chamber does not find it credible and give it no weight. Mr. Milosevic, if he has evidence that the witness perjured themselves, the Prosecution would not oppose the witness being recalled to face that evidence, to answer to that evidence. So underlying 92 bis is simply the principle of presentation of evidence and if the amici or the accused can articulate some area of questioning that they wish to put to this witness that seems plausible and reasonable to the Chamber, chances are the Prosecution would not oppose that witness being recalled and the Chamber certainly would be entitled to have that witness called. But I think 92 bis imposes some -- puts it to the accused and puts it to the amici to say why should the Chamber not accept the presentation of evidence in the form of transcript testimony? Why must the witness be recalled to give oral testimony once again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will consider this and give your ruling in due course. We will await the submission of the Prosecution document tomorrow. Mr. Nice, it's time for the adjournment unless there's something you want to deal with briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm in Your Honour's hands. Has the Court yet received the summary of the next witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Should I mention all administrative matters after the adjournment? I'll probably be about three or four minutes on administrative matters and a couple minutes on the next witness. It will be five minutes in all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Shall we deal with it now? If it's five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first thing I wanted to say had to deal with the witness list served last week. I hope it's self-explanatory, but I know that the accused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That hasn't found its way to us yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry about that. The motion did but not the witness list. The Chamber will recall that we were expelled from the building for technical reasons at 3.00 on the Friday, so it couldn't get on the -- on the Thursday, so it couldn't get in on the Thursday. I'll make my observations about the list when you've got it. It's silly to do it otherwise, and then the accused can perhaps follow the shape of the list which is designed to be helpful. One other technical point, procedural matter the witness Patrick Ball who was the expert called in the Kosovo part of the trial is being called back this week because of a corrigendum he wished to make to his report. He's not under an interdiction that he shouldn't talk to the Prosecution; nevertheless, I shall make it plain that my present intention is he may be spoken to by us briefly, or probably not at very great length so we can understand what it is that he's wishing to lay before the Chamber then either to, with the Chamber's leave, lead the evidence or alternatively just simply get him -- either lead the evidence or get him to explain the evidence himself. In relation to the forthcoming witness, it may help you if you have before you not only his statement or rather his summary but the exhibits for this reason: The witness who has the benefit of protection kept a diary. When he met the investigator, he provided the investigator with notes that were extracted from his diary. The diary is no longer available to him, but the notes extracted from the diary are, and indeed all of them, bar one page, have already been provided to the accused. The witness is in a position to speak about three meetings. The diary entries dealt with those meetings and the notes provided to the investigator are, broadly speaking, transcripts of those original diary entries. The notes provided have been marked in the margins in either red or blue. The red passages are passages which are by and large simply taken straight from the original diary entries which were themselves broadly contemporaneous. The blue notes are a different kind that the witness wrote in preparation for his encounter with the investigator. My proposal is that when we come to the evidence about the meetings in particular - there are three of them - the best course would be for the witness to simply go through his notes which are side-lined in red, and then to be asked one or two supplementary questions. This will save time but also be the most accurate reflection of the evidence which this witness is able to give. But I thought it helpful to give you advance warning of that being the course I was proposing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. So we can have the witness immediately after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. Oh, one other thing. One paragraph only does he seek to give - or two paragraphs - in closed session. It's on the second page -- or in private session, and I would ask for leave to call him on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration. If you would stand to do that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We didn't get an interpretation of that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English on this channel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Would you read it again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I start the evidence, the Chamber will note that the front page of the summary has a schedule of exhibits. There will be some corrections as to what was to be dealt with in public and what under seal. So it's only an indication. The Chamber will also see on the second and third page an idea hopefully enacted coming from this pact that you should have a dramatis personae of the people mentioned by the witness to which you may readily refer. I think one error has crept in on what is page 2. In the last entry of the box that says, "figures in the MUP and the state security service," the last entry there, the second sentence, "part of Backa Palanka lobby" should be deleted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And just to make it plain, the pseudonym, there seem to be a number of pseudonyms given to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For these purposes this witness is going to be known as C-048.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we deal with the background of the witness and by one paragraph that you can find in -- starting at the foot of page four but in the reality at the top of page 5, may we deal with that immediately in private session? It'll take little more than a few minutes, couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witnesses's exhibits be given --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness C-048, how was it that you first came into contact with the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: In early May 2002, I made contact at my own initiative, believing that I was familiar with certain circumstances and events which may be of assistance in this proceeding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you seek any benefit or gain from the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: I never asked for any kind of gain nor ever considered receiving it from the Prosecution or from this testimony because I'm convinced that it is the duty of any honest man to testify at court against crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness C-048, did you in May of 1992 get a job at a business in Belgrade called the MP Royal, which was a casino, restaurant and cafeteria, based in the Hotel Putnik -- I beg your pardon. In Novi Sad, not in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes. But I would like to make a correction here. The company was in Belgrade -- no, no, in Novi Sad. Belgrade was mentioned but the company was in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this hotel opposite the Regional Board of the SPS party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who owned this business?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Veselin "Vesko" Vukotic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Vesko his nickname?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Vesko Vukotic in due course tell you of what he had done in the 1980s in relation to Albanian immigrants in Europe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Vukotic told me about the liquidations of Albanian immigrants throughout Europe, that he did that on the instructions of the Yugoslav secret service. He particularly mentioned the latest, the most recent, the last recent that he committed, that was the assassination of an Albanian immigrant and human rights activist, Mr. Hadriu who lived in Brussels. He also mentioned to me on several occasions that that was the first assassination, political assassination, that the State Security Service of Serbia committed on its own, without any consultation with the federal service which still existed at that time and that practically constituted the beginning of the break-up of unified security system of Yugoslavia. Before he told me that, he told me he did that with the help of Andrija Lakonic and with the logistics support of Darko Asanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Staying with the liquidations in the 1980s, did Vukotic tell you what the general policy was as to which Albanians should be liquidated and why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Vukotic mentioned that in the 1980s, the general policy of the federal service was the liquidation of Albanian intellectuals because, without any intention of insulting the Albanian people, because the educational structure in general was quite low and the loss of any intellectual for them resulted in major harm. And as Mr. Vukotic was very picturesque in the way he expressed himself, there was a lot of time necessary for new intellectuals to grow up. And when he said weeds amongst them, he meant the Albanian intellectuals. Mr. Vukotic also said that in the 1990s, especially the mid-1990s, he criticised the policy conducted by the accused here and his police, which was based on mass repression of the Albanian population in Kosovo. Mr. Vukotic believed that the methods that were used before were much more effective because they did not result in animosity and the rage of the international community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I move on to a matter of detail? The murder of Enver Hadri, which was the first one traceable to the Serb DB and not to the federal organs, just to be clear, did Vukotic say precisely who had committed the murder?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: He told me very clearly that he committed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an investigation in Belgium into this killing? Were any arrests made? How did such an inquiry end?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: I know that the Belgian police conducted an investigation and that he was wanted by the Belgian police. Mr. Vukotic, until the 16th of November, 1997, did not travel abroad for the above-mentioned reasons. And then he left because he had to, because he had committed another murder in Montenegro in a place called Prcanj. I also know that in September 1995, in Greece, Darko Asanin was arrested on suspicion of involvement in the liquidation, but the entire Serbian and Yugoslav leadership at the time, both political and police leadership, got to its feet in order to get Darko Asanin out of prison. Marijan, the wife of Darko Asanin at the time, went to give a false statement that Darko was with her at the given time so that Darko could leave prison and then --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Thank you. And then as to the man Lakonic, I know this is in italics in paragraph 7, but in a sentence, what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Lakonic was liquidated in late March 1990 in a club, discotheque called Nana in Belgrade because he had become dependent on heroin, and he had begun to boast publicly about all that he had done for the service. Vesko Vukotic was given the task to do this. They did that in a way which caused a little bit more attention from the public, but Vesko Vukotic managed to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that -- that that you've told us of general background coming from Vukotic's mouth and other material you learnt connected to it in the course of your time with him. I now want to look chronologically at the first few months at any event in your time in the Royal casino. When you first went there, what was your job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: My first job was to control all the cashiers in the cafeteria and in the restaurant, and particularly in the casino because the owner Vesko Vukotic thought that the staff was stealing from him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What success did you have in your supervision of the staff? What promotion did it bring and why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes. The turnover increased suddenly, almost 50, 60 per cent. The owner was very satisfied. And then he also received positive recommendations about me regarding my studies, where my average marks were 10. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The promotion was to the position of general manager?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And although your details are protected and won't be revealed, this would mean you became general manager at a young age.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Shortly thereafter, did Vukotic, paragraph 17, approach you -- not shortly thereafter. Some months thereafter, did Vukotic approach you with a proposition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When and what was the proposition?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was in June 1992. He proposed that I should start cooperating with the state security service, and he told me that Milovan Popivoda would come and talk to me, and another person. He didn't say who that would be. He then said that Milovan Popivoda was the chief of the Novi Sad centre for state security and told me a few words about him, that he was very powerful, influential, and that he was a close friend of Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the meeting took place, where did it take place and who in addition to Milovan Popivoda attended?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Milovan Popivoda came, and Veselin Dakovic was with him who worked in the Novi Sad department of the centre for state security. It was the department for external extremism, which included Croatian extremism as they officially called it. They came to the cafeteria, the Royal cafeteria, during the day when we were closed because we only started to work in the evening. They introduced themselves to me and made their offer that I should work for the state security service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we've already had some evidence in this trial of the way in which the state security service penetrated all walks of life. Can you help us? Your position, your age, your understanding of these things, how usual or unusual was it that such an approach should be made to a person like you, in your position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: This was usual. Casinos, nightclubs, escort clubs were places that were especially of interest to the service, gambling places where all kinds of people circulate from all kinds of spheres. In other words, the underworld.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're going to hear in due course of how you got involved with the security service and what you did. From that, can you just -- so from your experience, can you just tell us this: Had there been a restructuring or was there a restructuring of the MUP that followed the constitutional changes in Serbia, and if so, what was the effect of that so far as the Novi Sad centre was concerned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: After the anti-constitutional putsch of October 1988 when the Vojvodina leadership was replaced and after that the same coup d'etat was repeated in Kosovo, constitutional changes were made and changes in the organisation of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia. Up until that time the provinces, as part of their executive councils, had their own Ministries of the Interior, an independent ministry which was in a coordination relationship with the republican ministry in Belgrade. And after the constitutional changes and the adoption of the appropriate laws, there were no longer provincial Ministries of the Interior but chiefs of public security and state security were appointed from Belgrade throughout Serbia. So the provincial ministries of the interior were officially abolished along with some other ministries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So therefore, what position, how important a position did Popivoda hold given his position at Novi Sad? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the Novi Sad state security centre was the biggest one in the province and also the biggest one after the Belgrade one in the whole of Serbia, and in view of the environment that I'm talking about, Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, as well as in view of the personal relationship and contacts of Milovan Popivoda with the members of the Backa Palanka lobby, so their friendships and other relationships, Milovan Popivoda was the informal chief of the state security service for Vojvodina, Eastern Slavonia, and Baranja, and he was the personal friend of Jovica Stanisic and others of whom I will be speaking about later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to tidy up in case I forget it later, your account of DB centres. In July of 1996, did Popivoda tell you what happened to the DB centres of Vukovar and Beli Manastir after the signing of the Erdut agreement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Popivoda told me that by the end of June, since our conversation was in July 1996, that by the end of June of that same year, the centres were dislocated from Vukovar, Beli Manastir, to Vojvodina, thinking of the technical equipment as well as the most -- the majority of the staff. And he responded clearly to my question. "Well, we will not leave these areas so easily to the Croats, will we." Mr. Popivoda replied to that, "Of course we will not. Our people will remain on the ground, but they will be working or operating under different circumstances."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That all emerged later in your relationship with Mr. Popivoda let's now go back to the beginning of that relationship when he met you with the man Veselin Dakovic. Who was Dakovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: He was an operative worker of the state security service. He was born in 1959 or 1960. I can't say exactly. But he worked in the sector for or department for internal extremism, and he was one of the leaders there. Personally, he was fairly intimate with Popivoda following the Montenegrin ties he had with them and some other people too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, now, in due course, Witness C-048, you are going to give us evidence of meetings at which you were present, involving very senior officials. This is your first encounter with Popivoda and Dakovic. Is there some significance of what happens later in how you were approached and how you responded at this early time do you judge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. As I've already said, they came to the Royal. Mr. Popivoda spoke first. He gave us a general overview of the historical situation, the historical times in which we were living, all the rest of it. And then after that he said that I was a good guy, a good student. He praised me. He said that I was working in a good company, that the proprietor was a good man himself. And he mentioned my salary which at the time amounted to 1.000 German marks, which for those times in Serbia a fantastically high salary. And he also said I knew people who were interesting to them security-wise and that it would be a good thing if I was to work for them, that is to say, observe and monitor those two individuals. And their names and positions were Marko Kljajic. That was the first one. And the priest in Petro Varadin, zupnik. And Petro Varadin is a part of Novi Sad. The parish priest. And they thought that they collaborated with the Croatian intelligence service. The other person was one of my best friends. We were of a similar age. His name was Robert Coban and at the time he was editor-in-chief of independent newspaper or rather weekly entitled Nezavisni Svet or Independent World.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just pausing there for a second. Now, you were basically being asked to provide information on two friends of yours, your contemporary Coban and the priest whom I think was several years older, Kljajic; correct?
