utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in short and we'll look at it in a few more sentences, but in short did you agree to do what was asked of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes, I did agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I said earlier, your reaction to this may feature as an element in your judgement in what you were allowed to observe later, but help us, what was your reason at this time, if you can now articulate it, for agreeing to work for the DB providing information on two friends of yours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Well, to be quite frank, at the time I accepted the offer made to me, I thought, "well, all right. I'll send in some general information." But I nevertheless began working on concrete issues straight away. The reasons were not political and -- were political -- were not political and ideological. It was quite contrary to what I did, and I'm really ashamed of that today. Can I describe the reason as being the pragmatism of life. Like any young man, I was enticed by the high salary and the possibility of a good life. At a time when most of my fellows had some very existential, very real material problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a second meeting after the first? If so, whereabouts was it held and how much later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes, there was. And it was soon afterwards. A week, ten days at the most after the first meeting, in the building of the Novi Sad centre of state security, which is located in Bulevar Oslobodjenja Street, next to the old building of the Nafta-Gas company, and that is where I had a meeting once again with Milovan Popivoda and Veselin Dakovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What passed between you on this occasion? What was said and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: On that occasion, I handed over a list of people who came to visit Mr. Kljajic and those that Robert Coban was in contact with, and that he saw that that was it, that I had started to collaborate properly, because the information they had up until that time coincided and were along the lines of what I told them. I told them who I had seen there. And after that, Mr. Popivoda started talking about the historical times we were living in and said that the goal was, the object was to have as many Croats leave Vojvodina as possible so that, as he put it, a stable border should be set up in the border belt between Vojvodina and Croatia, and, as he put it, with hard-line Serbs from Krajina. In that context, a particular thorn in his tied was the priest Marko Kljajic. And many of the parishioners who wanted to leave and go to Croatia, he would try and prevail upon them to stay in their own homes, on their own thresholds to look after their national identities, ethnic identities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Popivoda explain to you how this plan was to be effected? What methods were to be used to make people move?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: At that first meeting or, rather, the second meeting, but that's when he began to make concrete mention of these things, he said that the method should be used to intimidate the richest and well-to-do -- most well-to-do people in the villages where there was a majority Croatian population or where there were a considerable number of Croatian inhabitants. And once they saw that the most influential people and the richest people were leaving, the others would follow suit. He also said that violence and liquidation were not the methods of choice for Vojvodina. He even mentioned in a negative context the killing of an old man in a field in a place called Hrtkovci in Srem which took place in those days of June 1992. And his words were, "Look at what those idiots have done in Hrtkovci." He wasn't worried about the killing of the old man. He knew that this would cause problems with the international community and what the public reactions to it would be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he explain, with any further particularity or detail, why liquidations in Vojvodina were not acceptable? Did he contrast the position in Vojvodina with the position anywhere else in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: He mention that had they were not acceptable because Vojvodina was not a part of the battle area, the war area, and that as I've already said this would create problems with the international community, and if this did happen, for example, in Eastern Slavonia and Baranja, this could always be described to the anarchy that is customary when you have a war and things of that kind in those areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a third meeting? If so, where? Who was present, and what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: The third meeting took place soon afterwards, and in addition to Mr. Popivoda and Dakovic, Djordje Banjac was there too, and he was the head of the department, the technical department for bugging. I don't know what this was, the official title of it was, but I do know what it dealt with, bugging. And they asked me to bug the premises, both the offices and the residential premises of priest Marko Kljajic and Robert Coban, to set up a wiring system, and that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did this meeting with Popivoda, Dakovic, and Banjac occur?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: In the state security service building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the same office as for the second meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've set out in the summary the means you used to bug these two premises of your former friends, and you can give answers about the detail of that if asked. Is it sufficient to say you did manage to bug the premises that you were asked to bug?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Let me be more specific. I enabled the service to enter the premises and have their technicians place the bugging devices where they considered it to be necessary. I abused the confidence placed in me by the people who had up until that time been my close friends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware one way or another as to whether their telephones were intercepted or tapped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes. The service did do that via the post office from their central building. There was no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given any instructions as to your future conduct in relation to both of these friends or former friends of yours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes. I was told to tell them what they wanted to hear, and they explained to me how this sort of intelligence interview was to be conducted. And Milovan Popivoda would always stress, "Don't ask them anything. Just listen and they'll tell you everything themselves in due course, in the course of the conversation."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a particular incident at Kljajic's house in which you had an involvement and of which you can give a history and of which you hold a view, I think, a personal view?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes. At the end of December 1992, Milovan Popivoda told me, and I'm quoting his very words, that I should bear pressure on the priest to have him leave Vojvodina. End of quotation. They asked me to learn when Marko Kljajic was going to travel to Croatia, and that's what I did. I told them that the -- it was planned for the beginning of January. I can't give you an exact date now, but it must have been round about the Orthodox Christmas, one or two days before or after, in that period. And the two refugees -- two refugees attacked his house and attacked his mother. And she was an elderly lady of about 70. But she was fairly resilient despite her age, so she was able to defend herself, and her attackers finally fled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that event receive any media attention?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that event receive any media attention?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes, it did. The papers wrote about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What effect did that have on other Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: It was designed to have an effect and it quite certainly did. It instilled fear in the rest of the Croats, and they wanted to have them think that if they attacked the priest, what would happen to us? And Popivoda told me that the service incited the writings in the press about that event. They encouraged them to write about it. Not in the affirmative sense. They didn't write positively about it. But the message conveyed was quite clear. The message behind the newspaper articles was quite clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen to the men who to your knowledge had carried out the attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: They were taken into custody and brought to a police station, and some legal proceedings were started against them but nothing came of it as far as I know. And they were given a very mild conditional sentence of some kind. They didn't have to go to prison at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're still at the fairly early stage of your work for the DB. You carried on for several years, but tell us, did you ever have a DB identification card?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: No. I never carried an ID card. I had never had one, but I did have an emergency number, and it was 22862, and that was the number given to me for any emergencies. The area code was 021. That is the area code for Novi Sad. At that time there were no mobile phones yet, and when Mr. Popivoda got a mobile phone himself, he gave me his personal mobile phone number and it was 063201481.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As your relationship with Popivoda developed and continued, how regularly did you meet him, where? Who made reports, and did things change as to who made reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Let's take this step-by-step. I would have a meeting with him once or twice a month either at the Royal or in the DB centre. Sometimes he was alone. At other times Veselin Dakovic would be present as well. And reports -- the reports referred to the people visiting the priest, Marko Kljajic. They were most interested in Ivo Beslic who was a priest, a parish priest in Sremska Kamenica then there was Branko Melvinger who was the president of the democratic alliance of Croats of Vojvodina. Then there was Niko Kraljevic, the priest in Hrtkovci. Zeljko Garmaz who was a journalist at the time, and today he is an editor of the paper Vjesnik. He would go to Belgrade and Novi Sad fairly frequently and would always see the priest Marko. He was also interested in a person called Tomislav Basic who was an army retiree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that is enough for the targets of interest some of whom are dealt with at paragraph 32. As to reports, did there come a time when you prepared reports yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes, there did. At the beginning, Popivoda and Dakovic asked me to tell them word by word what I had been doing. When I got into the job, I talked about Popivoda and Dakovic was a younger man in terms of age and position and he would take down notes. But very soon I was able to differentiate between what was vital and what wasn't so important and I was able to write the reports myself after that. And so in addition to handing over the reports, we would also discuss other matters during our meetings. That is to say I didn't have to spend so much time reporting to them. I handed over my written reports.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you keep -- or did you keep copies of those reports or did you hand them all over to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: I handed them all over to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you instructed in writing or just verbally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Always verbally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout your time working for the DB, were you also working at the Royal casino?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you finish working for the DB?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: I stopped contact sometime in the year 2000, although from the end of 1998 they became less frequent in that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning then to the casino itself. Was it visited by several if not many famous people or people famous at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you list them really by frequency, that is, those who -- those important people who went there most frequently and then coming down to those who went there less frequently or only once? Of those who were regular attendees, can you tell us their names and just in a sentence what their role was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: They would come to the cafe or the restaurant of the facility. Milorad Vucelic came by mostly. Vucelic. The director general of Radio-television Serbia of the day. He had a party post as well. I can't tell you which one exactly. Then there was Milovan Popivoda, the head of the Novi Sad centre of state security. And his brother Milutin Popivoda, The director of marketing for Radio-television Serbia. Mihalj Kertes. Up until the end of August, there was the deputy Minister for Internal Affairs until the end of 1992. That was his official title, position. Then there was Radovan Pankov, one of the vice-presidents and later on the president of the provincial board of the Socialist Party of Serbia, the party whose president was the accused here. Another man who would come was Jovica Stanisic, the chief of the state security service of the MUP of Serbia. Then there was Franko Simatovic, nicknamed Frenki Simatovic, the commander of the special units or special operation units of the state security service of the MUP of Serbia. Then there was Marko Kekovic, director of television, Television Novi Sad. As well as many other medium-ranking officials. Jovo Barosevic, a case in point, who was director of the Posomi [phoen] Prostor company in Novi Sad. And it was through him that various illegal operations were conducted or operation with elements of protectionism.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you've given us several names. There may be one or two others that you can help us with. Is there any particular person or persons who came only infrequently or only once, to your knowledge, to the casino?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes. The person accused here, Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He came what, once or more than once?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Just once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come to the circumstances of that visit later. Can you help us, please, if you knew anything of the following people or ever saw anything of the following two people: Goran Hadzic, or the man known as Arkan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes, I did see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us a little bit about Hadzic, what you knew about him and what his visit or visits was like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Well, Goran Hadzic before the war, and this is common knowledge, was a warehouse clerk. He was the person of low intellectual and human capabilities, an individual who frequently used his position as so-called president of the so-called Republic of Serbian Krajina, the RSK. And one of his main goals, to be quite frank with you here, was to eat and drink without having to pay for it in restaurants. At the meetings that I'm going to talk about later on, he usually kept quiet. He was the classical type of puppet. And he didn't mind being in that position himself, because I assume he was aware of his very meagre and modest intellectual, moral, and human capabilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With which of the others that you've named --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With which of the others that you've named did Hadzic have most to deal, if it's possible to say and if it isn't we'll move on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: He had -- He mostly contacted with Frenki Simatovic, Mihalj Kertes, Milovan Popivoda.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I also asked you about the man known as Arkan. Can you tell us anything about him, and if you can, who he had contact with.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Arkan would come to the cafeteria several times privately to meet with Veselin Vukotic because they were friends otherwise, dating back to the 1980s. They did similar work, and both of them were from the crime scene, low-life and classical killers. I apologise, Mr. Nice, but do you mean Arkan's contacts with political leaders and so on? The next part of your question, what was it? Could you repeat?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the people you've already named as coming to the casino, if you were aware of his having any particular contact with any of them. If not, say so.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Well, I do know that he did have contacts with Frenki Simatovic, Mihalj Kertes. Mostly with those two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of all these people, setting on one side, please, the accused in this case, of all the others, which seemed to be the superior, the senior person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Milorad Vucelic and Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From your general conversation with these two -- sorry. Did you have conversation with these men yourself in your capacity within the casino or did you just see them at a distance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: On several occasions, I personally talked to them. Not so much with Jovica Stanisic, but with Milorad Vucelic I did during those years, right up to a year or two years ago when I saw him last. At least two or three times a month. I would meet him two or three times a month because that's when he would come by the Royal, because he was a close friend of the proprietor, Vesko Vukotic. And he was a friend and remains a friend today. He still maintains contact with those people who on the INTERPOL wanted list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did either of these men, Stanisic or Vucelic, speak of the accused to you when they spoke to you and if so in what context or setting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: They often mentioned him. Always mentioned him as chief. "Chief said this," or, "Chief said that." That's how they would refer to him in their conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did either or both of them indicate how easy or difficult it was for them to have contact with the accused?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Until 1995 in particular, when they wanted to get an accused, they were very close to him. They had cordial relations with him. And then in the mid-1990s, they said they were thwarted in this by the wife of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a few photographs to look at. I think, although I said there would be no need, to go into private session for the first two photographs with your leave which relate to the very short passage of evidence. At least one of them does that we've had in private session so far should be dealt with in private session. It will only take a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at this photograph. What was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: The outside. This is the club, the cafeteria, and casino Royal on the first floor of the hotel Putnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection. I don't understand why a photograph showing a singer and another person that is mentioned is being given at closed session as if it was some kind of secret photograph, and we're talking about a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will go back into closed session -- private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of whom is this a photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: This photograph from left to right, professional killer Veselin "Vesko" Vukotic. In the middle is an unknown person. And the next person is Milovan Popivoda, the chief of the Novi Sad state security centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next photograph, please. Who is shown here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: From left to right Vesko Vukotic and Milutin Popivoda, the marketing director of Radio-television Serbia and the brother of Milovan Popivoda.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, was that taken at the Royal club?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 55 of the summary. The topic is whether people with criminal connections came to the club. But I also want you, if you can, to help the Judges with a fuller picture, if you can give it, of any connections there may have been between criminals at the club and people from other walks of life, including politicians. First of all, did people with known criminal backgrounds visit the club?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you name one or two in particular? Deal with them one at a time and give an account of what you learnt of the individual's activities and history.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Darko Asanin used to come, Andrija Draskovic. Arkan would come from time to time. So I would say that these three people were the most colourful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's deal with --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's deal with Darko Asanin first. What can you tell us about him, and in particular of what enterprise he engaged in about which you hold a strong view.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Darko Asanin was born in 1958 in Belgrade. He was a criminal, a person from a criminal environment and an active associate of the state security service, also known for the fact that he liquidated political immigrants for the secret police. He was a cousin of Pavle Bulatovic, the federal defence minister. He had strong connections with all the people who would come to the Royal cafeteria and casino. As far as his activities, Darko Asanin in October 1997 organised a group of young men headed by Petar Divljakovic, AKA Pera Divljak, whose main task was to cause unrest in Montenegro prior to the forthcoming presidential elections. Darko Asanin sided strongly on the side of Momir Bulatovic in those elections. That is the option that was supported by the accused here as well. The boys who went in order to cause unrest in Montenegro were caught very quickly because Pera Divljakovic is a person of low intellect and he is not very capable of personally organising anything, so they were arrested right away. And Petar Divljakovic managed to escape in time and to hide. The persons who were caught in Montenegro told everything about the reasons why they were sent there and what their objectives were and this is also something that Darko Asanin personally told me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this particular passage can be found at paragraph 69 so we've taken care of that. But I want to come back to paragraph 57.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness C-048, staying still with Darko Asanin, is there another activity that he engaged in with regard to Croatia that you can tell us about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes. Twice in the course of 1993, I went on trips with him to the then-occupied territory in the Republic of Croatia, to Erdut. This occupied territory was called the Serbian Republic of Krajina even though this amounted to a classic occupation according to everything that was known at the time. He was a personal friend, as I said, of Frenki Simatovic and Mihalj Kertes and the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened and what did you learn of what was afoot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: You mean the trips to Erdut?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll come back to Erdut later. Can we go back to an incident? If I ask you about the use that was made of a checkpoint at Orasje, can you help us, please, with what you knew of an enterprise involving Asanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This is the most terrible thing that I had heard about during my cooperation with the service and the time that I socialised with those people. Darko Asanin, and he personally admitted this to me and this information was confirmed to me also, and I will talk about that later, he had the task of organising the transfer of large quantities of heroin into Croatia as a form of special warfare with the aim of destroying or weakening the fighting morale of the Croatian youth and generally in order to cause problems in Croatia, because it is well known that drug addiction causes other kinds of crimes as well. Darko Asanin clearly told me that this was being conducted through the checkpoint in Orasje, that they had their own man in Zagreb who was distributing enormous quantities of heroin throughout Croatia, whose name was Zeljko Sobot he was later killed in a conflict between the so-called Serbian and Albanian Mafia in Zagreb. This information was later come firmed to me by some people in Zagreb, specifically one person that I met in the office of the mayor, Zlatko Canjuga as well as by certain people from the criminal milieu. And if it's necessary, I can give you the names of all the people who confirmed this information for me. After I heard this - I'm going back to 1993 now when I heard this in Darko Asanin's house - I was horrified and flabbergasted because this monstrous activity bordered on Nazi type of activities. I asked Milovan, Milovan Popivoda, if this was possible. He first jumped up from his chair angrily and with the words - I apologise to the Court but I'm going to quote him - "Well, fuck him. I hope he's not saying that." Milovan Popivoda told me after that this was an idea of Jovica, and he said something to the effect, "Well, the Siptars in Belgrade are doing the same to us," which, to tell the truth, is true. And in their opinion, that was one of the most effective ways to conduct special warfare.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when it was said that the Albanians were saying they were doing the same to us or to them, whereabouts was it said and you seem to accept that this was true, whereabouts was it said that they were doing this, bringing drugs in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: In the same context, in the conversation in 1993 it was stated to me. And this refers to the period in the early 1990s when the price of heroin went down drastically on the streets of both Belgrade and Zagreb, and it was possible practically to buy these drugs for nothing practically. And it was accessible to everybody. And it was clear that this had not only a financial, material effect but also a political effect. Of course people in that chain, from the middle of the chain to the bottom of the chain worked only for material gain, and they didn't know what the whole thing was about. I don't have specific information that I could talk about the activities of the Albanian lobby or the Albanian immigration, however you want to call them. I'm talking about what the Serbian state security did through criminal elements in Croatia or as they said conducted special warfare. I also know that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Carry on then.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: -- That in February 2001, in the safe of the Komercijalna Bank in Belgrade, 600 kilogrammes of pure heroin were found dating from those years, without any kind of receipt of the -- about the origin of the heroin, why it was being there. And also, it is a fact that the state security service is not responsible for combatting drug trafficking. These drugs, and it was obvious to see clearly from the documentation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I think we'll just stick to what the witness can tell us about directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I ask one more question about Asanin, if the Court was looking at the clock?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How frequent or infrequent a visitor was Asanin to the casino, and did he mix with the other -- with the other people you've spoken of who have a political background?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: He came to the casino frequently as Vesko's best friend. These people also met at his house in Krnjesevci as well, and they also went to the exclusive club called Legat which was in Dedinje right next or right behind the Libyan embassy. The people who visited him were the following: Frenki Simatovic, Mihalj Kertes, Milutin and Milovan Popivoda. Bosko Ubojevic also came he was an official of the state security service as well. And of course Milorad Vucelic who got a gold Rolex worth 150.000 German marks from Darko Asanin about which the accused directly asked Vucelic here about where he got this watch from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Maybe I'd better deal with that after the break if there is to be one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn now. Witness C-048, you're giving evidence. Don't speak to anybody about it until it's over, and don't let anybody spoke to you, of course, and that does include members of the Prosecution team. Keep it to yourself until it's over. Very well. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 60, page 12.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The accused and the gold watch and the man Vucelic. Can you just give us a couple of sentences, a summary of that part of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes. This was a present that Mr. Vucelic received from the criminal Darko Asanin, a gold Rolex watch worth 150.000 German marks. When the accused heard about it he was very angry with Mr. Vucelic. He told him that in that way criminals -- in that way state functionaries are starting to work for the criminals and not other way around, which he thought was normal. Milorad Vucelic himself told me this. Darko Asanin was angry because Milorad responded to the accused Slobodan Milosevic that he got the watch from him. Darko Asanin said, "well, he could have said that he got it from Tom, Dick or Harry. Why did he say he got it from me?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Back to paragraph 55 in the summary, when asking you about criminals that visited the club you mentioned in addition to Darko Vucelic Andrija Draskovic. We haven't dealt with him in the summary but before I come back to him, was there a cousin of Vukotic known to you who had associations in the criminal world?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes. He was a cousin, Veselin Vlahovic, AKA Batica or Batko. Batica's brother had married Vesko's sister and Veselin Vlahovic, Batica, was brought to Sarajevo by Vukotic as a boxer. This is a person of very slight intellectual capacities. And not only that, it is a question of how sane that man is at all. He was a boxer in Sarajevo. Very soon he gave that up. He became involved in crime. At the beginning of the war, he joined the SDS paramilitary formations. He was a bodyguard of Momcilo "Momo" Mandic. He committed horrible crimes. He looted a lot in Sarajevo at the beginning of the war, and then he returned to Novi Sad where he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd just listen to counsel, please. Perhaps we could shorten the matter somewhat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you get your information of what Veselin Vlahovic had done?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Since this is a person if I may say who -- it's a question of how sane he is. He actually said that himself. He boasted with -- about those crimes, and he would also spend enormous amounts of money.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. Did you speak to him and he speak to you on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: We met a couple of times. I wouldn't call it a conversation. It was more him talking. I just sat there. I didn't want to contradict him or say anything because it seemed as if he wasn't all there. I would just say, "yes, yes." And on that occasion, he actually boasted about his Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, was he a person even known in the Sarajevo press by a nickname?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes. The Sarajevo press wrote about him in 2001 when he escaped from the Spuz prison, and there was also -- there were also reports that this Tribunal conducted an investigation about him. And should I explain why I said quote unquote or allegedly escaped from Spuz? Should I talk about that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'd just like you to give us his nickname and we'll move on to another topic for want of time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: We knew him as Batica at the Royal, but the Sarajevo press and the people in Sarajevo knew him by the nickname Batko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally you've mentioned Andrija Draskovic although his details do not appear in the summary. Just in a sentence, was he a regular visitor? What if, any criminality, was he connected to? But really, just a sentence or two at the most.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes. He was a regular visitor, and he was involved in crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us something of Frenki's attendance at Asanin's house. Was there an escort or prostitute facility connected with all this? If so, a sentence or so about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: If you're thinking about the Royal, yes, we did have such an agency. Formally, it was a fashion agency for the purposes of the public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were girls or young women provided for men? If so, whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes. They were models, but at the same time they worked as escorts. They were used for - how shall I put it? - for the satisfaction of the certain needs of politicians and other persons who came there. We didn't have special rooms where they would go, but they would meet there and contacts would be made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Then they would take them to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry my interjections have to be brief, but I mustn't allow you to speak at the same time my microphone is on. The question of drugs briefly. Were there any drugs in the Royal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: We were never involved in that. Vesko Vukotic nor I myself, but we provided narcotics for certain inspectors of the state security service which indulged in that kind of, let me put it that way, relaxation. And I'm thinking primarily as Veselin Dakovic who was a younger man. And also we were in constant touch with drug dealer Nenad Opacic who is currently serving a prison sentence for these crimes, who would come to the casino and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So far as the accused is concerned. We know there is only the one visit of which you're aware and you're going to deal with that later. Can you say anything about his knowledge of what his associates were doing by way of dealing or visiting this place which had a criminal element to it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: As I knew all the circumstances, it is quite certain that the accused, Slobodan Milosevic, knew that the persons mentioned came to the facility and that they socialised with Veselin "Vesko" Vukotic, Darko Asanin and the rest. Of course I can't claim that he knew all the details of that association, but in general terms, he knew where they were, who they were friends with, and what types of dealings they were involved in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge of or any contacts with the movements of his children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: His son Marko Milosevic, on the 15th of April, 1994, was at our discotheque when Zdravko Colic's album was promoted. And also I saw several photographs where Veselin Vukotic was with Marija and Marko Milosevic, standing together with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Red Berets, Your Honours, we've already dealt with paragraph 69. I'm going to deal with paragraph 71 before coming back to 64. I think it's more logical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the first time you heard Red Berets mentioned and in what context?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: I first heard it mentioned, that is to say when I heard those two words used, Red Berets, was in July 1992 when Jovica Stanisic and Milovan Popivoda came to the Royal where we were sitting around already, Veselin Vukotic and myself, and they talked about the formation of the unit. And that was the first time they mentioned those two words, Red Berets. As to the unit itself, I had heard about that before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From whom and what had you heard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: I heard it from Milan Popivoda, who said that at the end of 1991, a political decision was taken to establish a specials operation unit -- Special Operations Unit. And the reason was because on the battlefront in Croatia, there were a lot of units there, either under no control whatsoever or units which were not under the full control of anybody of the and they wanted to have a unit with a firm military organisation, a clear and strong chain of command, that is to say, based on the principles of subordination in which they could have complete trust and confidence. And he also mentioned in that regard that it was only Arkan's unit that was considered to be reliable, and that Seselj at that time was working, as he put it, for the same cause, and that in the barracks in Bubanj Potok, that is a place near Belgrade, Seselj's volunteers were being trained, and also that there were various paramilitary groups but that the service had to have a unit under its own control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we move on, to get a little more detail of this, can you just help us about notes? This is the first time where we may or the Chamber may find it helpful to look at notes. Did you keep some form of diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes, I did keep some form of diary, and it contain matters of this kind which were interesting to me and some private things as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you first met the investigator who took a statement from you, did you provide him with your own extract of entries from your diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: You mean to the investigators, whether I supplied them with a copy?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: The investigator saw it in my own home, but they didn't take the diary away with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later did you provide written, tract from that diary? Not extract, notes of and extract from.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I handed them over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In preparing to give evidence, have copies of those notes been marked in the margins with either a blue or a red or possibly in one case a blue and a red line indicating, so far as the red is concerned, that this is material pretty well taken not verbatim but taken directly from your diary, the blue passages being passages which are notes you simply made in preparation for speaking with the investigator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't invite the witness necessarily to have any part of his diary with him for this passage of his evidence. But for your assistance, if you're interested in following it, it's page 11 in the English of 12, and it is, for the accused if he wants to find it because he may do, it's page 6472, the last four digits, in the B/C/S version if he wants to follow it there. But I'm not inviting the witness to look at it on this occasion, although, as I've said, I will when we come to the meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Then tell us please, Witness C-048, when you first heard of this group later described as the Red Berets, were they given any name and who was in charge of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: No specific names were mentioned. Milan Popivoda said that for the needs of the Red Berets, they had either released part of the criminals from the prisons or they were amnestied and didn't have to serve their prison term.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was in charge of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Frenki Simatovic was in charge of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you may have told us this. I'm afraid I haven't checked it off. Can you explain just in a sentence the political decision, if there was one, by which this group was set up and the political purpose or the political/military purpose of this group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Of course a political decision was made. A political decision had to be made for the establishment of a unit of that kind, and that decision was made at the end of 1991 to set up units which would be within the framework of the security service and the purpose of which would be to act on the front, on the battleground in Croatia first and later on in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anything said about the man Seselj and any groups associated with him? If so, by whom was it said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Milovan Popivoda said this. Seselj was mentioned in a positive context, but he added that he wouldn't be allowed to have his unit just like that or, rather, that he did work at the time to the advantage of the general cause, as he put it, but the service wanted to have a unit of its own under its full control. And he also said that Seselj's volunteers were trained at the barracks in Bubanj Potok but he also emphasised you never knew how Seselj might turn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not in the summary, but is there any other group of a like kind or broadly similar kind that you can give or that you can remember being spoken of by name? Any other named group of paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Mention was made of the White Eagles, Beli Orlovi. The Dusan Silni detachment, and Bokan's White Eagles in the context of anarchy. And of course Arkan's unit was mentioned in that context too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anything said about -- by whom these groups were supplied with arms, and if so, who said it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: It was mentioned on several occasions, and they said that Frenki was the main person in charge of the distribution of weapons to Arkan's unit. As far as Seselj was concerned and his volunteers, they said that the training was being done in Bubanj Potok, which was a military establishment, a barracks, and that they were receiving weapons from the regime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now back, please, to paragraph 64 of the summary, page 13. Did you see anything of people whom you understood to be Red Berets at the Royal? If so, who and on what frequency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes, I did see them. I saw Zivojin "Zivko" Ivanovic and he was best known by his nickname Zika Crnogorac or "Zika the Montenegrin" and he would come by most frequently because he knew the proprietor from earlier on and he was also a Montenegrin like the proprietor. And there was Petar Divljakovic, and he was better known as Pera Divljak. And on one occasion I saw and met Dragan Mijovic too, and I knew him from when the time I did my regular military service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these men or any of them speak of their activities in the Red Berets? If so, what did you learn from what they said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes, they all talked about it. Zika Ivanovic "Crnogorac" would talk about his time in the Red Berets. Pera Divljakovic, Pera Divljak would brag about the crimes he had committed. And he is also not fully accountable as a person. To explain to the Court what kind of man this was, after everything, he didn't end up in a mental hospital but he did end up in a monastery at Fruska Gora. He was of diminished responsibility and liked to drag about his crimes and even exaggerated in my opinion, because in the atmosphere that prevailed during those days in Serbia, especially in that particular environment, crimes against the Croats and Muslims were heralded as some form of prestige.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell us of anything you heard about any Red Berets about activities qualifying if you feel you should by your assessment as to whether the person concerned was exaggerating what he claimed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Petar Divljakovic mentioned specifically in more concrete terms the massacre of Croatian policemen, and he called them and referred to them as Ustashas. At the end of November nearby Borovo Selo where 20 people were killed and thrown into the Danube. And he said that he had done that with a group of friends or, rather, with his unit. And there was another friend of his called Ivan Andric, and in my opinion, he didn't exaggerate that event. But he did exaggerate a massacre at Mostar where he said that they had killed over a hundred Ustashas and balijas. The balijas, I am quoting that term. It was a term he used to refer to the Muslims by. Petar Divljakovic, in the context of the rest of the Croats in eastern Croatia, as they called it the RSK, Republic of Srpska Krajina or, rather, the occupied territory of the Republic of Croatia, he said he would have killed them all but Frenki didn't allow him to do so. End of quotation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want now to move to meetings. Was there a meeting in August 1992 that you can recall and of which you made notes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I just be allowed --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: I was going to explain the reasons for their meeting and how this informal group operated, because I think we skipped over that. About the Backa Palanka lobby, that's what I'm thinking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to skip over it but I want to raise something with the Chamber first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Court will find the notes of this part at page 5 of the notes. The accused can find it at pages 6455 to 6458 if he wants to follow it in the notes. I would ask that the witness can have the document in front of him if he wishes, either to refer to it or even frankly to read from it as a more efficient way of getting the detail. But it's a matter for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just so I can understand it, although it's called a diary, these are essentially notes which he's made from the diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: With interpolations which he himself has more recently put in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. As I understand it is simply an explanation of what was in can -- either explanation or a transcription of or a transcription and an expansion so as to make sense of notes that are contemporaneous and essentially complete. The passages sidelined in blue are notes that he's drawn from his memory more generally. So that if we look at page 5 and I shan't rehearse --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, did you mention where the original diary is now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I didn't and I should have done and I'll get the witness to deal that straight away and then we'll come back to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness C-048, I should have asked you. Forgive my oversight. The original diary itself, where was it when you last saw it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: It was in my own home, and the investigators were able to see it when they came to visit me at the home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you left your home, did you leave the diary there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: I apologise, but may we go into private session and I'll tell you why?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness have before him his own notes opened at page 6455.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And C-048, you've been told that you are free to refer to those notes but in reality I think only the one sidelined in red if you wish to, and if becomes more helpful effectively to follow them as you give your evidence to save time do so and we can fill out details you miss after you've given your evidence. But before we come to the notes themselves, you wanted to say something about the Backa Palanka lobby represented at the meeting in August 1992 to which we turn. Explain that lobby to us, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: When I speak about the Backa Palanka lobby, what I mean is a certain lobby that was made up of individuals from the police, the secret police, the information and propaganda realm of the political apparatus and the crime -- criminals. And they all the worked together, harmonised and dovetailed their activities and implemented the orders of the here accused. And also among them was a high degree of personal solidarity, and I can quote numerous examples to bear that out if you need to hear them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who do you identify as member of this lobby, the Backa Palanka lobby?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: The members of the Backa Palanka lobby were the following individuals: Mihalj Kertes, Radovan Pankov, Jovica Stanisic, Milorad Vucelic, Marko Kekovic, Milovan Popivoda, Milutin Popivoda, Frenki Simatovic, and also Brana Crncevic who was a writer. He was close to them too. And then there were criminals, Veselin "Vesko" Vukotic and Darko Asanin. But Darko Asanin distanced himself a little while later from these individuals to a certain extent. So if you allow me, this was the link between the police, the secret police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Carry on. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: It was the police, the secret police, the information and propaganda department of the political apparatus and criminals as well. It linked all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This first meeting in August 1992 was attended by whom from that lobby?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Jovica Stanisic attended as did Milorad Vucelic, Milovan Popivoda, Mihalj Kertes, Goran Hadzic and Veselin "Vesko" Vukotic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we come to what was said, paragraph 99 of the summary, why would you, a young man, although now running this casino, why were you allowed to be present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: As I've already stressed, after some concrete operations I gained their trust. They also knew that as Vesko's number one man, they could place their trust in me, have confidence in me. Of course I didn't take part in the discussions at the meetings, nor did I talk to them. It was just my job to see that they were all served, to -- I don't want you to think that I was a waiter, but I wanted to have waiters collaborate with the pauses, when they had pauses that they were all served, and that they were served whisky, and Chivas Regal was the make of the whisky that was most often served.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you ever given advice, and if so by whom and to what effect about whether you should talk about what you heard at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: The -- first of all, Veselin Vukotic and Milovan Popivoda told me in a well-intentioned form that I shouldn't speak about this at all. It never entered my head actually, because I knew that that same man Veselin Vukotic two years ago had killed Andrija Lakonic, somebody he had grown up with. So I could have imagined how easy it would have been for him to kill me had I started to talk about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Back to paragraph 83 of the summary and what you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Back to paragraph 83 of the summary on page 16. Witness C-048, tell us, please, what was said. Take your own course. If you read from or are guided by the notes that we have of course also in translation, please remember that it's easy when reading from something to read much faster than you speak and therefore it's difficult to go at a speed that is acceptable to the interpreters. So take your own course but tell us, please, what was said at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: This was an informal meeting. When I say "informal," there were no minutes taken, but it had concrete and clear-cut goals and intentions and it discussed concrete issues. Jovica Stanisic started to talk first. He said that he had just come back from the boss, and the word "boss" referred to the accused here quite clearly. And he said that on -- at the London conference forthcoming there, would be mention, and I quote as he said, "Our territory is in the Republic of Serbian Krajina." And this referred to the occupied territories of the Republic of Croatia. Mihalj Kertes said he was going to do everything to clean out -- that a lot of Ustashas had already gone. And Jovica Stanisic emphasised that this was essential for negotiating positions to be adopted at the forthcoming London conference. So that with the policy a fait accompli, these territories should be conjoined with the Republic of Serbia. Jovica Stanisic then told Mihalj Kertes that he should work in as subtle a manner as possible to avoid any human casualties and that he was to proceed by first intimidating people in a certain region, a few people to begin with to instil fear in them and then the others would follow suit. He underlined the difference between the methods that were to be applied in Vojvodina and the methods in eastern Croatia, that is to say, the UNPA zone as they were officially called. And he also said that they should leave no traces behind. He also told him about the -- that on the territory of Serbia, family homes should not be blown up. Mihalj Kertes's answer was that he should maintain constant cooperation with Frenki Simatovic, and he also mentioned the liquidation of an old man in Hrtkovci at the end of June 1992 in a negative context, as an example of what should not be done. And on that occasion, I also heard that the object of the policy being pursued, that is to say to use a fait accompli to effect territorial domination, but mention was also made of the other parts of the so-called Republic of Serbian Krajina and the context of negotiations can be held in that respect and that the eastern regions would "always be ours," as they put it. Milorad Vucelic said in addition to the general political phrases that he used that propaganda was patriotic and he worked in the sphere of information to promote it and he also said and I apologise for having to say this, the scum like my former kum, Mile Isakov are always around. Let's me explain that to Your Honours. Mile Isakov was the president of the independent association of journalists of Vojvodina at that time. Jovica Stanisic also said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In order for us to take this in it would be sensible to break it up. It's very difficult to take in a narrative of this sort that simply flows along. Perhaps if you would break it down it would assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm certainly happy to do that and it may be that the witness, I know the handwriting on the document is not -- it's his handwriting so you can follow it. The one that's marked in colour is a little faint. You've also got the original there for him. What I'm going to do on Your Honours' page 5 of the notes, I think we've covered everything up until about ten lines from the end and we then covered most of that that the witness was becoming more free in style. And so I'll go back and ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, C-048, you were dealing with what Kertes said that they should be in constant contact with Frenki, and you then said that he said how the accused had said that such -- no. I beg your pardon. Said that liquidation were is not to be carried out in Serbia. Just tell us who said liquidations were not to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes, Jovica Stanisic said that. While Kertes replied to Jovica before that that he was in constant contact with Frenki.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Then you've mentioned propaganda?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who said anything about propaganda as opposed to liquidations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Milorad Vucelic talked about propaganda because he was the person in charge of propaganda as well as the director of the national television. He was talking about patriotic propaganda, that he was doing everything in the informational sphere. And then he mentioned, as he said, and I apologise to the Court, "Scum such as my cousin Mile Isakov are always around."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pausing there. You mentioned reference to the eastern provinces and how they should be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Overall and look at your note, please, because you've got it there in front of you, was reference made to Eastern Slavonia, Western Srem and Baranja, it's in shorthand I think in the original, and then just tell us please the next sentence what was said and refer to a passage in quotation marks if it's appropriate and tell us who said that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: When we're talking about the eastern regions, I'm thinking of the area that was officially called Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, and that is the eastern region of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And looking at your notes, just tell us exactly who said what about how those areas must be cleansed from Ustasha?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Jovica Stanisic began first. He said that he had been to see the boss, as he put it, and that at the London conference there would be discussion of, I quote, our --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you'd look please at your own notes. It's obviously not entirely easy to find it but I'll do my best. Immediately after a passage where you refer to the incident in Hrtkovci at the end of June 1992. If you find that passage, keep your finger on it and if you follow me through your own notes we'll deal with things in an orderly way. Can you find that note?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you would be good enough then to go to the next sentence which deals with -- well, the end of that sentence deals with Vojvodina, intimidation, and propaganda. Go to the next sentence which begins he said that the Eastern Slavonia, Western Srem and Baranja must be cleansed from the Ustashas. Tell us who was speaking and what was said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Jovica Stanisic said that, stressing the methods of activities in eastern Croatia and in Vojvodina itself. He said that the so-called Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem should be cleansed of the Ustashas and then the Croats may ask to get that region as much as they can, but they would never get it. Also, it was mentioned, as I also said at the beginning of my testimony, that in the border region of Vojvodina, a stable Serbian majority must be formed with resilient Serbs as they put it and this is something that I also heard from Milovan Popivoda at our second meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stay with the first meeting. Keep your finger on the notes if you'd be so good. Was it at this stage that Vucelic said something about a patriotic mission? And just look at the next sentence and tell us what it was he said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes. Vucelic said that we were all on a great patriotic mission, that we have to create a strong Serbian state with as few hostile elements as possible, that he is doing everything in his power in the information sphere, that he believes that the propaganda on RTS was patriotic. And then I quote, "Scum like my former kum, Mile Isakov are always around."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Keeping your finger on the notes, was it Milovan Popivoda who you next recall joining the discussion, and if so, top of our page 6 in the English version, what was it that was said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Milovan Popivoda joined the discussion, and he said that a network of intelligence centres was formed in the region he called Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem and that he was monitoring those intelligence centres. That was the first time that I heard directly from his mouth that he was practically the real chief of the intelligence services of the so-called Republika Srpska Krajina in the eastern part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do your notes go on to record an intervention or an observation by Jovica Stanisic next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes. Jovica told him that the boss said that they should not worry about money because there always has to be money for the needs of the service and for such things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there discussion about Milan Panic? If so, to what effect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes. They talked about him. The Federal Prime Minister at the time. They said that the accused here, Slobodan Milosevic, regretted nominating him to the post of prime minister, and they said that the objective of the accused here, Slobodan Milosevic, in connection with appointing Milan Panic was for him through his connections with the US administration should act for the abolishment of the sanctions, and he believed that Milan Panic would not really interfere much in the actual running of the affairs, but it had turned out differently, that Milan Panic did not agree as a person of integrity to be a puppet. And they said that he would very soon be removed from his post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when Hadzic left the meeting, and did Stanisic ask Kertes something at that stage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes. Goran Hadzic went to the toilet, and Jovica Stanisic asked Kertes, "Are you and Frenki keeping this one under control?" To which Kertes replied that he shouldn't worry. And Jovica said, "Good. Good. I don't really want to think that he's really the president."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next meeting --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next meeting, I think, was held in September 1992 that you can help us with; is that right? And again recorded in your notes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes. The same people were present. This time Frenki Simatovic was also there, as well as Radovan Pankov. I just want to emphasise Veselin "Vesko" Vukotic was always present at these meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll follow the same routine if this is helpful to the Chamber. Keep your finger really on the note so that you can go through it in the same orderly way that we can follow it in our translations of your handwritten notes. I take it this meeting was also at the club -- at the casino, rather.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did it start off with reference to the removal of Mihalj Kertes from a particular position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes. Mihalj Kertes, in the course of the London conference, was dismissed from his post as deputy of the federal Minister for Internal Affairs upon the instructions of Milan Panic. And this was done because of the ethnic cleansing that he had committed. This was an official decision by Milan Panic and it was given as the reason for his decision. They criticised this decision by Milan Panic. And in a way they kind of joked with Mihalj Kertes. They were on good terms with him and they were kidding him that he was now unemployed and so on. They said that Milan Panic was a traitor, that his activities should be prevented and so on. But also they said that luckily they were not being asked to do anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Stanisic then speak to Frenki? If so, what did he say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes. Jovica Stanisic addressed Frenki by saying, "The boss told me today to step up the actions in Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem because I heard that the Croats would try to enter Krajina by force by November 1st. He said that UNPROFOR was there but we also have to be ready so nothing surprises us there. And then Frenki replied, "Jovica, don't worry. Everything is under control."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Jovica Stanisic speak again to Frenki?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes. He told him clearly to quiet down his guys and make that Pera Divljak talk less. What can I tell you when it has even reached my ears, referring to the already mentioned Petar Divljakovic from the Red Berets who stuck out because of his brutality and during his leave while under the influence of narcotics and alcohol he used to say all kinds of things. Frenki said, "don't worry, I'll handle that. But you need to understand that they're young fellows, and without them we wouldn't be able to achieve anything." So he said that in order to balance out the situation and to defend those young men a little bit to which Jovica Stanisic told him, "All right. I do understand that, but still you should take care of it." And he said that in that context. Also, that he shouldn't worry about any financial or material resources.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the conversation return to Milan Panic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes. They --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Conversation with one of the Popivodas? I think you better tell us from your notes which of the brothers it is. It may not be clear. On your account it's only Milovan who was present, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Keeping your finger on the notes --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One moment. That's the end of -- that's the end of really this conversation unless the witness has been triggered by reading his notes to remember anything else material that he hasn't yet told us about. Is there anything else that you can remember of this conversation beyond what you've already told us that's material?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: As far as I have been able to follow my own testimony, I think that so far I have said everything that needed to be said. Popivoda was there, but he didn't really participate in the conversation so much so that I would remember it. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And perhaps you ought to tell us this: In what part of the club and if you can remember in what part of the day did these two meetings take place? First the first meeting. What part of the club? What part of the day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: The part of the club that was marked private. So it was a part of the restaurant. And it was early afternoon, between 12.00 and 1.00 p.m.. The reason why the meeting was held in that section was quite ordinary. It was summertime, so it was the most comfortable area to sit, because at that time of the day, the sun does not hit that part of the premises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That, I think, was the first meeting. What about the time and place of the second meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: The second meeting was held at the same place at a similar time. It was in mid-September in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We come to the -- Your Honour, we come to the third meeting. It can be found at the handwritten notes for the accused 6451, and in the English version it's page 8 of 12. Witness C-048, was there a meeting in March 1993 that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where and at what time of the day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: The Royal club, and the time of day was around noon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who attended?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: The accused here, Slobodan Milosevic, Milorad Vucelic, Radovan Pankov, Mihalj Kertes, Jovica Stanisic, Milovan Popivoda, Marko Kekovic, Veselin Vukotic was there the entire time. I was there also in the same role that I had at the already mentioned two previous meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From where had those attending this meeting come as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Not only did I understand it, but I saw it because from the place where Veselin Vukotic and I were before that, we could see that clearly. The named persons came from the provincial board of the Socialist Party of Serbia where the accused here was on a working visit. Milorad Vucelic, two or three days before that, told Vesko that he would see if he could bring the boss over. Of course he wasn't able to promise that because nobody could force or order the accused here to go and -- go anywhere. But still, Milorad managed to do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Using the same procedure, please, with your, as it were, finger literally or mentally on the appropriate part of the page, which in the version that's got numbers on it is the page that starts 6462, and the passage begins to the effect of "After they'd seated themselves, Pankov said." Can you then read out -- or not read out, tell us what happened at the beginning of the meeting when Pankov spoke.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes. Radovan Pankov was the first to speak, which was normal because at that time, Radovan Pankov was the number one man of Slobodan Milosevic for Vojvodina. Radovan Pankov with a large degree of humility said, "Well, boss, as I told you, the situation is under control." The accused replied, "Very, very well, Raso. I just want you to know that this is a very sensitive area. There are many minority groups here and plenty of hostile elements amongst them."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next? Who spoke next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: After that, the accused here looked in the direction of Jovica Stanisic and asked him about the situation in Eastern Slavonia and Baranja, to which Jovica Stanisic replied that everything was going according to plan, that the terrain has been cleansed of Croats and the security situation on the field -- on the ground was stable, to which the accused here said, "Very well. So we have completed the main part of the job. Carry on like that, but in a subtle way," and with a certain amount of pleasure he said, "Well, I'm really looking forward to how the Croats would ask for the Krajina as now where the majority of the population now are Serbs."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the last sentence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jovica Stanisic just shook his head and said, "Yes, yes. Very well."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The interpreters missed the last part of what you were saying, so can you go back to your notes and pick it up from the accused saying, "Well, we've completed the main part of the job," and go through your notes fairly slowly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes. I'll just continue. He said, "Just continue working like that, but in a subtle way." And then he said with a certain amount of pleasure, "And now, Bre [phoen], I would like to see how the Croats would ask for the Krajina from me when the Serbs are living there now, just the Serbs are living there now, especially Eastern Slavonia and Baranja. And as for the rest, we can still talk about it."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it at that stage that Stanisic shook his head and said, "yes, yes," or, "Very well"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next, to whom did the accused next speak?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, there's apparently another sitting in here at half past two, so we have to bear that in mind. No doubt we can sit for a few minutes longer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This passage of evidence lasts another four pages, so I'll see how far we can go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did the accused next address?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: He addressed Mihalj Kertes with his nickname, which was Bracika. He told him, "Bracika, you and Frenki just continue in this manner. You've done well so far. And as far as the material equipment is concerned, just ask Jovica for everything you need and Milovan is there also if you need him." And he was thinking of Milovan Popivoda. Then he directly asked Kertes, "Is Arkan under control?" To which he received the reply, "Yes, he is." And the accused here then said, "Very well. Very well. You just keep him under control. Don't let him gain control over you in due course. We need people like this now, but no one should think that they were more powerful than the state."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next thing said, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048
utterances.text: Then the accused here said that all kinds of pressure must be maintained and a united Serbian state must be made comprising the Republic of Serbia, Montenegro, Republic of Srpska, and the Republic of Srpska Krajina. And that is why it was important to stand all the pressures, because then the world would have to acknowledge the factual situation. He continued with the explanation that the Croats who once go towards Zagreb or to some European country have once found an apartment there or a job, in other words have fitted into that society will no longer want to return to the area where they originally came from. Also, he stressed that by using Republika Srpska and the Republic of Srpska Krajina, it will be easier for him to keep Montenegro under control in case they started to make waves, as he put it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Might that be a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope the Court has got or will have access to the witness lists. I can will deal with their formation probably more conveniently tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. It may be there are matters that have to be dealt with in relation to the next witness and the form that his evidence is going to take. Perhaps those responsible could look into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have the problem in mind. But I can tell you straight away that the witness's attitude is unchanged from what it was on the previous occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now. Nine o'clock tomorrow morning.
